emigrate

EM-uh-grayt -- from Latin e- ('out') + migrare ('to move, migrate'). · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To emigrate is to move from one's country to another.

Her grandparents chose to emigrate in the 1950s, leaving behind everything they owned for the promise of steadier work.

Example

A family sells their small farm, packs everything they own into three suitcases, and emigrates by ship, never to live in their home country again.

To emigrate is exactly that -- to leave one's own country permanently and settle somewhere else.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

defect: To defect is to abandon your own country -- usually secretly, and usually for political reasons, like a chess player slipping away from government minders during a tournament abroad. To emigrate is open and ordinary by comparison: you leave your country to settle in another, papers in hand, with no betrayal implied.

flee: To flee is to run from danger -- war, flood, arrest -- with escape itself the whole point. To emigrate is a planned, deliberate move from your own country to a new one; emigrants may spend months arranging papers and tickets. You can flee across town, but you emigrate only across a border.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

immigrate: to move into a new country to live there permanently

remain: to stay in the same place without leaving

Where it sits · how big an upheaval the move is

relocate → emigrate → resettle

relocate vs. emigrate: Relocate is a broader, more neutral word -- a family can relocate across town or across the ocean, for any reason -- while emigrate specifically means leaving one's own country permanently to live in another.

resettle vs. emigrate: Resettle often implies an even more difficult, large-scale transition than emigrate, frequently used for refugees or entire communities rebuilding their lives in a new country after being displaced.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — e-: out (a form of Latin ex-)

Root — migr: to move from one place to another (from Latin migrare)

Suffix — -ate: verb-forming: to do or make (Latin -atus)

Put it together: E- ('out') + migr ('to move from place to place', from Latin migrare) + -ate (verb ending) spell emigrate: literally to 'move out' of one's own country -- the mirror image of immigrate, which uses in- ('into') for moving into a new one.

Use the root in a new word: migrate: Rangers closed the north beach for a month to protect the migratory birds nesting there.

Root Check

Word Choice

Emigrate is very commonly confused with immigrate -- the two describe the same move from opposite points of view. You emigrate from your home country, and you immigrate to your new one; the direction of the prefix (e- 'out' vs. im- 'in') matches the direction of the move.
